- design: Create a design canvas — a multi-artboard visual design published as an Artifact that runs Claude Design's canvas editor (an early preview of Claude Design inside Claude Code). You DRAFT the design as .dc.html artboards laid out on one pan/zoom canvas; where saving is enabled for the user's account they refine every element visually (click-to-select, a properties panel, inline text editing, undo/redo) and Save publishes a new version for everyone, otherwise they get a view-and-export (PNG/PDF) preview of your draft. Good for UI mockups and screen flows, landing pages, marketing and social graphics, and print pieces — posters, flyers, brochures as single-page artboards; memos and reports as one flowing artboard. Use when someone wants a design, mockup, wireframe, UI or screen design, landing page, poster, flyer, brochure, banner, card, one-pager, or any visual layout they would rather tweak by hand than in code. Only for CREATING or re-seeding a canvas; an existing one is edited in its published Artifact.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".

- artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts — when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, keeping state shared across viewers, handing the viewer a file to save, or updating and republishing itself. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever the user asks for an artifact needing any such runtime behavior.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.

Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review. For ultra on a GitHub.com PR target, --post asks to post the finished review’s findings to the PR as a single comment from the user’s GitHub account (not a review; the launch dialog still confirms in interactive sessions, while non-interactive mode posts on the flag alone) and --no-post hides that option.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.

Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").

3	# The cold-reader prompt, ready to paste
4	
5	This file belongs to the `text-audit` skill, whose body is [`../SKILL.md`](../SKILL.md). One test in the body decides whether a finding blocks: the reader could not go on, or would have applied the text wrongly. The body's section "The cold reader" lists the kinds most blocking findings fall into. It also says who reads under this prompt and what to do with what comes back.
6	
7	This prompt prints every rule bound to human prose whose owner is a skill: 39 of the 66 rules the rule home carries. The rules at [`human-prose-rules.md`](human-prose-rules.md) name every other class an audit holds a text to. Judging those classes needs a rulebook the cold reader does not hold. The prompt's last instruction takes every other stop the reader met, so a class the printed list does not name still comes back.

9	Paste the block below verbatim into the cold-reader session, under that one test for a blocking finding, with the text appended.

11	```
12	You are reading a piece of text for the first time. You have no background on it: no
13	project history, no earlier draft, no knowledge of what the author meant beyond the words
14	on the page. Read it once, straight through, as a stranger who needs to understand it and
15	act on it.
16	
17	Mark every place you stop. A stop is any one of these:
18	- an ordinary word carrying a private project meaning — would a person outside this project recognize this word, or does the text gloss it in plain words where it first appears?
19	- a coined, loan-translated, or respelled word standing where a plain standard word exists — does a standard word already name this thing? Is the word used here that standard word, written as a real word of the reader's own language?
20	- a name stacking two nouns with no relation between them — does this name run two nouns together, and can a reader say how the second relates to the first?
21	- one thing answering to a second name — does any thing named here appear under a different word somewhere else in this document or its neighbours?
22	- a predicate applied to a subject that cannot carry it — can the thing this sentence names as its subject perform this verb, or hold this quality?
23	- a number standing with no ground — can a reader say what this number is measured against and which way is better?
24	- a set pointed at by a count, a pointer, or a position, with its members never given — can a person who reads this sentence alone name the members of the set it points at?
25	- a text breaking a rule it states — does the sentence stating this rule obey the rule it states?
26	- a word grading how important or how good a thing is — does this sentence tell the reader how much to care about what it reports?
27	- a sentence grading the person, or grading the writer's own act — does this sentence carry a fact, or a verdict on the person's remark or on the writer's own work?
28	- a sentence carrying no information — does the reader do anything differently because this sentence is here?
29	- a word inflating a statement while adding nothing — does removing this word change what the sentence says?
30	- English that reads as compressed or poetic — could a native technical writer have written this sentence for an open-source project?
31	- the person an explanatory sentence speaks in — does this sentence tell the reader what they do, in words spoken to them?
32	- a sentence with no actor, or its action buried in a noun — does this sentence answer who does this, to what, and when? Does its action live in a verb?
33	- a judgment with no judge and no measure — who decides whether this is true, and by what measure?
34	- a relational word leaving its slot empty — relative to what, by what measure, or else what alternative?
35	- a pronoun with no antecedent in its own sentence — can a reader say which thing this pronoun points at without looking back a sentence?
36	- an example restating a rule that was already clear — could a reader have read this rule two ways without this example? Does this example stand in prose, outside a rule entry in the rule home?
37	- an abstraction standing where a concrete noun would do — can the reader picture the thing this noun names?
38	- a paragraph carrying more than one point — does a reader who reads only the first sentences of this section still follow it?
39	- a reply that buries its answer — can the reader stop after the opening block and still hold the answer?
40	- an offer to do work the writer could already derive — does this sentence offer to do something the writer already has everything to do?
41	- a mistake expanded into a self-audit paragraph — does this passage explain the writer's own failure at more length than the fix takes?
42	- a working note handed to the reader unmarked, or a choice with no open answer — can the reader tell at a glance which lines are notes, and can they answer outside the options given?
43	- a task subject written in machine words — does a person glancing at this task subject know what is being done?
44	- one fact stated a second time in another place — does another place in this project already state this fact?
45	- a defect recorded as examples with no class behind them — does the entry state what the mistake is, so a writer can find an instance nobody has met yet?
46	- a sentence open to two readings, or hiding its cause or what it leaves out — can a reader read this sentence one way only, name what it makes happen, and say which alternatives it passed over?
47	- a thing named by its number, so the reader must leave the sentence to learn what it is — does this sentence say what the thing is? Does it give only a number, a position, or a count the reader must go and resolve?
48	- parallel items run together inside one sentence — does this sentence run several items together where a list would put one on each line?
49	- a rare word standing where an everyday word says the same thing — would a professional reader whose first language is other than English reach for a dictionary on this word?
50	- a document written in the register of the message that asked for it — did this sentence take its tone from the message that asked for the work?
51	- a placeholder word standing where the thing's own name fits — does this word name the thing, or does the reader have to carry the name in from an earlier sentence?
52	- a step naming a check, a file, or an act with no way to run it or find it — could a reader carry out this step from the page alone, with nothing else on hand?
53	- a set claimed whole while the text carries members outside it, or leaves members out with no reason — does the text's own list agree with the claim made over it?
54	- a claim resting on ground the reader of the page cannot reach — can a reader holding this page alone see what this claim rests on?
55	- a number stated without the four parts a measurement carries — reading this number alone, do I know what is counted, which decision it informs, and which command gives it again?
56	- a sentence carrying a second rule or a definition — does this sentence state one rule a reader could cite on its own, with no definition folded into it?

61	3. what a stranger cannot tell from the page alone;
62	4. the guess you made in place of the missing answer;
63	5. blocking or non-blocking.

66	list. If you stopped nowhere, say so in one line.

69	to what? by what measure? or else what alternative? A word the list above does not name, that
70	still stopped you, is a real find — report it and note that it is new.

4	
5	This page states every rule this project holds its own texts to, in the words a writer applies to a sentence. 11	## The words on this page
12	
13	The words these rules are stated in. Every page built from this home carries this block, so a reader holding one page holds every word that page uses. A word is defined here when two or more pages need it; a word one page alone needs is defined on that page.
14	
15	- **class** — the shape of a mistake: the form it takes wherever it turns up.
16	- **break** — one place a text falls short of a rule, being a single instance of the class that rule names.
17	- **catcher** — whatever finds a break: a literal pattern in a script, a model reading for meaning, or a person reading the text.
18	- **home** — the one file a given fact is written in.
19	- **the rule home** — the file `guardrails/language-rules.json`, where every rule is edited and nowhere else, and from which every page here is built.
20	- **rule** — one statement about one class, written as one entry in the rule home.
21	- **surface** — a kind of text rather than a file, so one file carries several; this project names six, and each rule binds the ones it applies to.
22	- **stop** — one place a reader could not go on, had to read twice, or had to guess.
23	- **a blocking stop** — a stop where the reader could not go on with the text, or would have acted on the text wrongly; every other stop is one the reader noticed and read past.
24	- **register** — the rules a surface's text is held to: which words, which sentence shapes, and how it addresses its reader.
25	
26	Five roles appear wherever these rules are discussed.
27	
28	- **the writer** — whoever drafts a text: a person, or the agent working for one.
29	- **the reader** — whoever reads that text afterwards, carrying whatever context they happen to have.
30	- **a cold reader** — a reader given the text alone, with no repository, no earlier drafts, and no way to ask the writer a question.
31	- **the maintainer** — whoever builds the catchers and repairs them.

A text declares one primary surface, and a text published to someone outside the project carries `artifact` as well, with every rule binding either surface in force. 76	## The words these pages use
77	
78	A rule's **status** says whether anything catches a break of it today.
79	
80	- `held` — a catcher runs this rule today: at a named harness event, inside a gate, or at a named manual step.
81	- `stated-only` — no catcher runs this rule, which includes a script that exists and is armed nowhere.
82	- `claimed-but-absent` — some file names a catcher for this rule, and that catcher does not carry it.
83	
84	Each **catcher** under a rule carries a status of its own.
85	
86	- `held` — this catcher runs the class it names over the surface it names.
87	- `partial` — this catcher reads part of the class, or part of the surface.
88	- `absent` — no catcher of this kind runs the rule.

90	**Armed at** names the moment a catcher runs, and what a break costs there.

92	- `pre-commit` — a gate refuses the commit until the text changes.
93	- `pre-push` — a gate refuses the push until the text changes.
94	- `session-stop-hook` — the session's reply is held at the end of the turn, and a correction is asked for before the text reaches the reader.
95	- `session-prompt-hook` — the verdict on the previous reply is put in front of the session when the person sends their next message.
96	- `PreToolUse` — the next tool call is denied, so the correction reaches the reader inside the same turn; a rule armed here records it in its notes, since the `armed` field's vocabulary holds no word for the event.

98	- `nowhere` — no catcher runs the rule at any event.
99	
100	A rule's **owner** names the one thing that decides a break of it. The status words above say what runs today; the owner says what is meant to run.
101	
102	- `script` — a literal check decides a break of this rule on its own.
103	- `skill` — deciding a break needs a model reading the text for meaning.
104	
105	No rule on this page carries a status, and that is deliberate: a rule binds a text whether or not a machine checks it. The words above are defined here because `docs/language-rule-coverage.md` states them of every rule.

107	## The rules
108	
109	### r01 — an ordinary word carrying a private project meaning
110	
111	**Rule.** A word keeps its everyday meaning. A term this project needs holds one glossary entry, written in plain words. The body then uses that term unchanged, with no definition attached.
112	
113	**Reader test.** Would a person outside this project recognize this word, or does the text gloss it in plain words where it first appears?
114	
115	**Binds.** spec-body · human-prose · chat · artifact
116	
117	**Examples.**
118	
119	- `The system shall red a branch whose merge-base sits behind main's tip.` → `The system shall refuse a branch whose merge-base sits behind main's tip.`
120	- `a landing` → `a change that reached main`

122	**Exceptions.** a term the text glosses in plain words at its first use; a term holding a glossary entry the reader meets before the term's first working use.
123	
124	### r02 — a coined, loan-translated, or respelled word standing where a plain standard word exists
125

635	### r40 — a conditional leaving a case unaccounted for

655	### r43 — an abstraction standing where a concrete noun would do

662

667	### r44 — a paragraph carrying more than one point
668	
669	**Rule.** One paragraph carries one point, stated in its first sentence, with the rest supporting it.

679	### r45 — a long flat run of peer items at one level

681	**Rule.** A document is a tree of grouped topics, and its levels nest without skipping. A long run of peer items is gathered under headed parents.

689	- `a bullet running the rule, its script, and its grep fallback together in one paragraph` → `the rule as the bullet, with the script and the grep fallback nested under it`

691	### r46 — a reply that buries its answer
692	
693	**Rule.** A reply opens with the answer: the outcome, the decision, or the finding. The opening runs a few lines, and the reader may stop there. Reasoning, evidence, and options stand underneath.

695	**Reader test.** Can the reader stop after the opening block and still hold the answer?
696	
697	**Binds.** chat · human-prose · artifact
698	
699	**Examples.**
700	
701	- `a report opening with the method it ran, and the finding in its last paragraph` → `the finding in the opening lines, and the method underneath it`
702	
703	### r47 — a clock time in a reply read from anywhere but the clock
704	
705	**Rule.** Every reply leads with a bracketed clock time, and every moment spoken to the human is read off the clock at write time.
706	
707	**Reader test.** Was this time read from the clock now, or continued from an earlier one?
708	
709	**Binds.** chat
710	
711	### r48 — an offer to do work the writer could already derive
712	
713	**Rule.** A derivable act is done and reported done. A backlog item is parked for the human only after a fresh test of whether the answer can be derived now.
714	
715	**Reader test.** Does this sentence offer to do something the writer already has everything to do?
716	
717	**Binds.** chat · human-prose · worker-brief
718	
719	**Examples.**
720	
721	- `just say the word` → `do the act and report it done`
722	- `let me know if you want me to` → `do the act and report it done`
723	
724	### r49 — a mistake expanded into a self-audit paragraph
725	
726	**Rule.** A mistake is owned in one line and fixed.
727	
728	**Reader test.** Does this passage explain the writer's own failure at more length than the fix takes?
729	
730	**Binds.** chat · human-prose
731	
732	**Examples.**
733	
734	- `Direct answer: yes, I broke the method... (a paragraph auditing my own failure)` → `name the fix in one line, make it, and go on`
735	- `Прямой ответ: да, я нарушил метод... (a paragraph auditing my own failure)` → `name the fix in one line, make it, and go on`
736	
737	### r50 — a working note handed to the reader unmarked, or a choice with no open answer
738	
739	**Rule.** Dense working notes are marked so the reader can skip them, and they carry one idea per line. Every choice offered leaves room for a free-form answer.
740	
741	**Reader test.** Can the reader tell at a glance which lines are notes, and can they answer outside the options given?
742	
743	**Binds.** chat · human-prose · artifact
744	
745	**Examples.**
746	
747	- `a dense working note handed to the reader with no mark on it` → `the same note opening with a marker that says it is a working note, one idea per line`
748	- `a dense working note handed to the reader with no mark on it` → `the same note opening with «(себе)», one idea per line`
749	- `a question offering two options and no third` → `the same question, with a free-form answer left open`
750	
751	### r51 — a question of the reader's left unanswered or buried
752	
753	**Rule.** A question that went unanswered during the work, or an answer buried inside a long reply, is recapped in one short line at the message's end.
754	
755	**Reader test.** Did the reader ask anything this message answers only in passing, or not at all?
756	
757	**Binds.** chat
758	
759	### r52 — a task subject written in machine words
760	
761	**Rule.** The harness task panel on the human's screen speaks plain product words in the documents' language, understandable at a glance.
762	
763	**Reader test.** Does a person glancing at this task subject know what is being done?
764	
765	**Binds.** human-prose · chat
766	
767	**Examples.**
768	
769	- `run gen-language-consumers.py and splice AUDIT_SKILL_REL` → `print the writing rules into the audit skill`
770	
771	### r53 — human-facing prose drafted by a writer holding the project's own vocabulary
772	
773	**Rule.** The first draft of prose a human will read is written by a fresh writer with no package rules loaded, working from a plain brief. The brief states the facts, names the intended reader, and lists the rules binding the surface. A person who has read the rulebook then reviews and revises that draft.
774	
775	**Reader test.** Was this sentence first written by someone who had never read this project's skills, working from a brief?
776	
777	**Binds.** human-prose · spec-body · artifact
778	
779	**Examples.**
780	
781	- `a paragraph drafted by the session that held the whole pack loaded` → `the paragraph drafted by a fresh writer from a plain brief, then revised by someone who has read the rules`

784	
785	### r54 — a changed section shipped before two clean cold readings
786	
787	**Rule.** A changed section is read by fresh readers who carry no project context, until two consecutive reads return zero blocking findings. `skills/text-audit/SKILL.md` defines a blocking finding.
788	
789	**Reader test.** Did a reader with no project context read this section and stop nowhere?

792	
793	**Examples.**
794	
795	- `a section shipped after one reading that returned five stops` → `the section read again after the repairs, and shipped once two readings in a row returned nothing that blocks`
796	
797	**Exceptions.** the cold reader running a read is handed the section while the bar is still unmet, since a read is how the bar gets measured.
798	
799	**Thresholds.** consecutive_clean_reads = 2.

801	### r55 — an anchor, marker, heading, or literal changed by a rewrite
802	
803	**Rule.** A rewrite leaves anchors, marker lines, headings, and literal classes standing verbatim. Every difference is named and verified.
804	
805	**Reader test.** Does every anchor, heading, number with a unit, backticked path, and quoted sentinel appear exactly as it did before?
806	
807	**Binds.** spec-body · artifact
808	
809	**The lists this rule names.**
810	
811	- *the literal classes a rewrite leaves standing* — 4 members, read at build time from `scripts/spec-freeze.json` under `literal_classes`:
812	    - an anchor citation in square brackets, such as `[INV-141]`, `[E-26]` or `[INV-28 kin]`
813	    - a bare range token, such as `T-1..T-7`
814	    - a number carrying a unit: px, GB, MB, s, a day count, a percentage, or a ratio such as `4:3`

818	    - any H3 heading (`### `) carrying a square bracket

820	### r56 — one fact stated a second time in another place
821	
822	**Rule.** One fact lives in one home. Every other place points at that home.

827

829	
830	- `the writing rules written out a second time inside another skill` → `the rules in one file, and the second skill pointing at that file`
831

834	### r57 — a phrase the human cut returning in a later draft
835	
836	**Rule.** A phrasing the human cut in a review round stays out of every later draft of that artifact. An approved text takes exactly the correction the human named.
837	
838	**Reader test.** Has the human already cut this wording from this artifact?
839	
840	**Binds.** human-prose · artifact
841	
842	**Examples.**
843	
844	- `«X — not Y» returning in a later draft, after the human cut it` → `the sentence saying what the thing is, in its own words`
845	
846	### r61 — a defect recorded as examples with no class behind them
847	
848	**Rule.** When a text stops a reader, the writer names the class of mistake, defines it, and enters that class in the rule home. The examples under an entry are the recorded evidence that produced the class.
849	
850	**Reader test.** Does the entry state what the mistake is, so a writer can find an instance nobody has met yet?

852	**Binds.** spec-body · human-prose · chat · artifact · commit · worker-brief
853	
854	**Examples.**

856	- `a list of banned words: leg, goes red, station, door` → `the class - a coined word standing where a standard word exists - with those four as its recorded evidence`
857	- `a list of banned words: «нога», «краснеет», «станция», «дверь»` → `the class - a coined word standing where a standard word exists - with those four as its recorded evidence`

859	### r62 — a sentence open to two readings, or hiding its cause or what it leaves out
860	
861	**Rule.** A reader reaches one interpretation of a sentence, sees what causes what, and can tell what the text leaves out.
862	
863	**Reader test.** Can a reader read this sentence one way only, name what it makes happen, and say which alternatives it passed over?
864	
865	**Binds.** spec-body · human-prose · chat · artifact
866	
867	**Examples.**
868	
869	- `it hands the text to a fresh reader who has no knowledge of its history and marks every place a stranger stops` → `it hands the text to a fresh reader who knows nothing of its history, and that reader marks every place a stranger stops`
870	
871	### r63 — a thing named by its number, so the reader must leave the sentence to learn what it is
872	
873	**Rule.** A sentence names a thing by what it is, and its number trails at the line's end.
874	
875	**Reader test.** Does this sentence say what the thing is? Does it give only a number, a position, or a count the reader must go and resolve?
876	
877	**Binds.** spec-body · human-prose · chat · artifact
878	
879	**Examples.**
880	
881	- `Requirement 233 states the orchestration laws.` → `The requirement on how work is routed between tiers states the orchestration laws [INV-241].`

883	- `the four laws` → `the four laws — worker-routing, lean-orchestrator, pull-unblocked-work, and classify-the-subtask`
884	
885	**Exceptions.** a number trailing at a line's end as an anchor, which is what rule r11 already governs; a numbered step inside a procedure the reader is currently walking.

889	**Rule.** Two or more parallel items become a bulleted or numbered list under a one-line lead, one item per line.
890	
891	**Reader test.** Does this sentence run several items together where a list would put one on each line?

893	**Binds.** spec-body · human-prose · artifact

897	- `The system shall refuse a branch behind main's tip, a lane with no open row, a host with no worktree line, and a lane past the cap.` → `The system shall refuse each of the four faults below.
898	- a branch behind main's tip;
899	- a lane with no open row;
900	- a host with no worktree line;
901	- a lane past the cap.`
902	
903	**Exceptions.** two items a single short clause carries without strain.
904	
905	### r65 — a rare word standing where an everyday word says the same thing
906	
907	**Rule.** A sentence takes the everyday word wherever an everyday word carries the meaning. A rare or bookish word stands only where no everyday word says the same thing. A term of the profession stays as it is, and the words around it come down.
908	
909	**Reader test.** Would a professional reader whose first language is other than English reach for a dictionary on this word?
910	
911	**Binds.** spec-body · human-prose · chat · artifact
912	
913	**Examples.**
914	
915	- `a writer marinated in this project's own vocabulary` → `a writer who has already read this project's rules`
916	- `the loop is armed at a named harness event` → `a hook runs the check when the session ends`
917	
918	### r66 — a document written in the register of the message that asked for it
919	
920	**Rule.** The register of a request settles nothing about the register of the document. A person writes a request however is fastest for them. Every document is written to the rules of its surface, whatever the request looked like.
921	
922	**Reader test.** Did this sentence take its tone from the message that asked for the work?

931	
932	**Rule.** A term defined in one home stands in another file only where that file gives its reader a path to the definition. A file read on its own carries the terms it uses, or it names where each one is defined.
933	
934	**Reader test.** Reading this file alone, could I reach the definition of this term?

940	- `together with the settings ladder` → `together with the four scopes that settle a setting: the session's live word, the host profile, the personal profile, and the package default`
941	
942	### r68 — a placeholder word standing where the thing's own name fits
943	
944	**Rule.** A sentence carries the name of the thing it is about. A pronoun or a general word stands only where the name would clutter the sentence. A status word stands only where the sentence has already stated the condition behind it.
945	
946	**Reader test.** Does this word name the thing, or does the reader have to carry the name in from an earlier sentence?

950	**Examples.**
951	
952	- `This keeps the leading context clear enough to hold the campaign.` → `The leading session then holds enough room to carry the campaign.`
953	- `The second goal needs its own measure` → `The growing specification has no measure today`
954	- `A report says which documents are done` → `A report says which documents are measured clean and read clean`
955	
956	### r69 — a step naming a check, a file, or an act with no way to run it or find it
957	
958	**Rule.** A step the reader has to carry out names the command that runs it, or the path that holds it. Where the text can name neither, it says so and names what the reader does instead.
959	
960	**Reader test.** Could a reader carry out this step from the page alone, with nothing else on hand?

962	**Binds.** spec-body · human-prose · artifact · worker-brief
963	
964	**Examples.**

966	- `the structure checks over requirement shape, the generated index, the matrix references, and the frozen baseline` → `each of the four checks on its own line, with the command that runs it`
967	- `the project's own copy of the list otherwise` → the project's own `guardrails/weak-words.json`, created with a `weak_words` list where the project holds none
968	
969	### r70 — a set claimed whole while the text carries members outside it, or leaves members out with no reason
970	
971	**Rule.** A claim that a set is complete states what the set covers and what it leaves out. The list printed under such a claim carries every member the claim names.
972	
973	**Reader test.** Does the text's own list agree with the claim made over it?
974	
975	**Binds.** spec-body · human-prose · artifact
976	
977	**Examples.**
978	
979	- `These are every rule binding human-prose.` → `the rules binding human prose, with the printed count and the reason a code is missing`
980	
981	### r71 — a claim resting on ground the reader of the page cannot reach
982	
983	**Rule.** A claim carries its ground on the page that makes it. A file named beside the claim holds the record, and the page still states what the reader needs.
984	
985	**Reader test.** Can a reader holding this page alone see what this claim rests on?
986	
987	**Binds.** spec-body · human-prose · chat · artifact
988	
989	**Examples.**
990	
991	- `The loop came from the spec-format comprehension gate.` → `what that gate observed, stated on the page, with the file that records it named beside it`
992	- `that run is clean` → `the command that runs the check, and what a passing run prints`

994	### r72 — a number stated without the four parts a measurement carries
995	
996	**Rule.** A number stated to a reader carries four things. They are why it is measured, what changes when it moves, its unit, and the method behind it. The four stand in the number's own sentence or in the paragraph around it. A number quoted from a named source inherits that source's method.

998	**Reader test.** Reading this number alone, do I know what is counted, which decision it informs, and which command gives it again?
999	
1000	**Binds.** spec-body · human-prose · chat · artifact
1001	
1002	**Examples.**
1003	
1004	- `A reading returned fifteen stops.` → `name the unit, the decision the count informs, what changes when it moves, and the command behind it`
1005	
1006	### r73 — a sentence carrying a second rule or a definition
1007	
1008	**Rule.** One sentence states one rule and holds no definition.
1009	
1010	**Reader test.** Does this sentence state one rule a reader could cite on its own, with no definition folded into it?
1011	
1012	**Binds.** spec-body · human-prose · artifact
1013	
1014	**Examples.**

1017	
1018	**Exceptions.** a rhetorical triad, which carries no list.
1019

1021	
1022	**Rule.** Every domain noun the body uses holds one glossary entry of one sentence.
1023	
1024	**Reader test.** Does the glossary hold an entry for this noun, and does that entry come before the noun's first working use?
1025	
1026	**Binds.** spec-body
1027	
1028	**Exceptions.** a word of ordinary English, which needs no entry.

1030	### r75 — a normative sentence binding a vague actor
1031	
1032	**Rule.** A normative sentence names the actor it binds, and that name is the actor that acts.
1033	
1034	**Reader test.** Does this requirement name the actor it binds, and is that the actor that acts?
1035	
1036	**Binds.** spec-body
1037	
1038	**Examples.**
1039	
1040	- `the system` → `the actor that acts, where the document names a finer one`
1041	
1042	**Exceptions.** a region marked informative.

1044	## An index of questions

1092	- r08 — a sentence running past the word cap for its surface

### r65 — a rare word standing where an everyday word says the same thing

**Rule.** A sentence takes the everyday word wherever an everyday word carries the meaning. A rare or bookish word stands only where no everyday word says the same thing. A term of the profession stays as it is, and the words around it come down.

**Reader test.** Would a professional reader whose first language is other than English reach for a dictionary on this word?

**Binds.** spec-body · human-prose · chat · artifact

**Examples.**

- `a writer marinated in this project's own vocabulary` → `a writer who has already read this project's rules`

- an ordinary word carrying a private project meaning — would a person outside this project recognize this word, or does the text gloss it in plain words where it first appears?
- a coined, loan-translated, or respelled word standing where a plain standard word exists — does a standard word already name this thing? Is the word used here that standard word, written as a real word of the reader's own language?
- a name stacking two nouns with no relation between them — does this name run two nouns together, and can a reader say how the second relates to the first?
- one thing answering to a second name — does any thing named here appear under a different word somewhere else in this document or its neighbours?
- a predicate applied to a subject that cannot carry it — can the thing this sentence names as its subject perform this verb, or hold this quality?
- a number standing with no ground — can a reader say what this number is measured against and which way is better?
- a set pointed at by a count, a pointer, or a position, with its members never given — can a person who reads this sentence alone name the members of the set it points at?
- a text breaking a rule it states — does the sentence stating this rule obey the rule it states?
- a word grading how important or how good a thing is — does this sentence tell the reader how much to care about what it reports?
- a sentence grading the person, or grading the writer's own act — does this sentence carry a fact, or a verdict on the person's remark or on the writer's own work?
- a sentence carrying no information — does the reader do anything differently because this sentence is here?
- a word inflating a statement while adding nothing — does removing this word change what the sentence says?
- English that reads as compressed or poetic — could a native technical writer have written this sentence for an open-source project?
- the person an explanatory sentence speaks in — does this sentence tell the reader what they do, in words spoken to them?
- a sentence with no actor, or its action buried in a noun — does this sentence answer who does this, to what, and when? Does its action live in a verb?
- a judgment with no judge and no measure — who decides whether this is true, and by what measure?
- a relational word leaving its slot empty — relative to what, by what measure, or else what alternative?
- a pronoun with no antecedent in its own sentence — can a reader say which thing this pronoun points at without looking back a sentence?
- an example restating a rule that was already clear — could a reader have read this rule two ways without this example? Does this example stand in prose, outside a rule entry in the rule home?
- an abstraction standing where a concrete noun would do — can the reader picture the thing this noun names?
